claim: Autocatalytic activation of EGFR coupled to dephosphorylating activity of protein tyrosine phosphatases (PTPs) ensures robust yet diverse responses to extracellular stimuli.
source: Autocatalytic activation of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) coupled to dephosphorylating activity of protein tyrosine phosphatases (PTPs) ensures robust yet diverse responses to extracellular stimuli.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract summarizing the system's properties, based on the study's findings and established knowledge about EGFR signaling.

claim: The tradeoff of EGFR plasticity is spontaneous receptor activation and spurious signaling.
source: The inevitable tradeoff of this plasticity is spontaneous receptor activation and spurious signaling.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by the experimental data showing spontaneous EGFR phosphorylation in the absence of ligand.

claim: A ligand-mediated switch in EGFR trafficking enables suppression of spontaneous activation while maintaining EGFR's capacity to transduce extracellular signals.
source: We show that a ligand-mediated switch in EGFR trafficking enables suppression of spontaneous activation while maintaining EGFR's capacity to transduce extracellular signals.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experiments showing differential trafficking of liganded vs unliganded EGFR.

claim: Autocatalytic phosphorylation of tyrosine 845 on unliganded EGFR monomers is suppressed by vesicular recycling through perinuclear areas with high PTP1B activity.
source: Autocatalytic phosphorylation of tyrosine 845 on unliganded EGFR monomers is suppressed by vesicular recycling through perinuclear areas with high PTP1B activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by FLIM-FRET data showing EGFR-PTP1B interaction in perinuclear regions, Rab11 knockdown experiments showing increased Y845 phosphorylation, and FRAP/FLAP experiments demonstrating recycling.

claim: Ligand-binding results in phosphorylation of the c-Cbl docking tyrosine and ubiquitination of the receptor.
source: Ligand-binding results in phosphorylation of the c-Cbl docking tyrosine and ubiquitination of the receptor.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and immunofluorescence data showing increased Y1045 phosphorylation and ubiquitination upon EGF stimulation.

claim: EGF-induced EGFR self-association is required for c-Cbl-mediated ubiquitination.
source: This secondary signal relies on EGF-induced EGFR self-association and switches suppressive recycling to directional trafficking.
evidence: This is supported by anisotropy data showing EGF-induced dimerization and ubiquitination experiments showing that PV-induced phosphorylation without dimerization does not lead to efficient ubiquitination.

claim: The re-routing of EGFR regulates signaling response by the transit-time to late endosomes where it is switched-off by high PTP1B activity.
source: The re-routing regulates EGFR signaling response by the transit-time to late endosomes where it is switched-off by high PTP1B activity.
evidence: This is supported by FLIM-FRET data showing EGFR-PTP1B interaction in perinuclear regions, trafficking data showing EGF-induced movement to late endosomes, and mathematical modeling.

claim: This ubiquitin-mediated switch in EGFR trafficking is a uniquely suited solution to suppress spontaneous activation while maintaining responsiveness to EGF.
source: This ubiquitin-mediated switch in EGFR trafficking is a uniquely suited solution to suppress spontaneous activation while maintaining responsiveness to EGF.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the mathematical modeling and experimental data showing that the system cannot function properly without the trafficking switch.

claim: EGFR signaling is implicated in embryonic development, tissue homeostasis and wound healing.
source: EGFR signaling is implicated in embryonic development, tissue homeostasis and wound healing (Yu et al., 2010; Sibilia et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: EGFR overexpression and hyper-activation through genetic alterations have been linked to malignant transformation.
source: while EGFR overexpression and hyper-activation through genetic alterations have been linked to malignant transformation (Rowinsky, 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Mutation-induced loss of autoinhibitory interactions or enhanced receptor expression levels frequently elevate the basal phosphorylation and activation status of EGFR.
source: Mutation-induced loss of autoinhibitory interactions or enhanced receptor expression levels, frequently elevate the basal phosphorylation and activation status of EGFR (Arteaga and Engelman, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The autoinhibitory interactions include the tethered conformation of the extracellular domain.
source: The autoinhibitory interactions include the tethered conformation of the extracellular domain (Ferguson et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Autoinhibitory interactions include receptor-membrane interactions and the local intrinsic disorder of the αC helix in the N-lobe of the kinase domain.
source: as well as receptor-membrane interactions and the local intrinsic disorder of the αC helix in the N-lobe of the kinase domain (Arkhipov et al., 2013; Endres et al., 2013; Shan et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Autoinhibitory interactions create an energy barrier for EGFR self-association that is surpassed upon ligand stimulation.
source: This creates an energy barrier for EGFR self-association that is surpassed upon ligand stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited structural studies and the known mechanism of EGFR activation.

claim: Ligand binding leads to receptor dimerization.
source: Ligand binding leads to receptor dimerization (Yarden and Schlessinger, 1987; Cochet et al., 1988)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ligand binding leads to the formation of an asymmetric dimer of the intracellular kinase domains.
source: and the formation of an asymmetric dimer of the intracellular kinase domains (Zhang et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Ligand-induced dimerization triggers phosphorylation in trans of regulatory and signaling tyrosine residues in the intracellular part of the receptor.
source: This triggers phosphorylation in trans of regulatory and signaling tyrosine residues in the intracellular part of the receptor
evidence: This is established knowledge about EGFR activation mechanism.

claim: Phosphorylation of EGFR leads to subsequent recruitment of adaptor proteins that contain Src homology 2 domains (SH2) or phosphotyrosine-binding domains (PTB) such as c-Cbl (Y1045) or Grb2 (Y1068 and Y1086).
source: and a subsequent recruitment of adaptor proteins that contain Src homology 2 domains (SH2) or phosphotyrosine-binding domains (PTB) such as c-Cbl (Y1045) or Grb2 (Y1068 and Y1086) (Ushiro and Cohen, 1980; Moran et al., 1990; Levkowitz et al., 1998; Waterman et al., 2002; Lemmon and Schlessinger, 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Despite EGFR structure intrinsic safeguards, the receptor can still attain an active conformation in the absence of ligand due to thermal fluctuations.
source: Despite these EGFR structure intrinsic safeguards, the receptor can still attain an active conformation in the absence of ligand due to thermal fluctuations (Lemmon and Schlessinger, 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and is consistent with the experimental observations of spontaneous phosphorylation.

claim: Spontaneous EGFR activation necessitates only low protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTP) activity to suppress phosphorylation due to this 'leaky' kinase activity.
source: necessitating only low protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTP) activity to suppress phosphorylation due to this 'leaky' kinase activity.
evidence: This is supported by the mathematical modeling and experimental data showing that low PTP activity at the PM can suppress autonomous phosphorylation.

claim: Phosphorylation of the conserved regulatory tyrosine Y845 in the activation loop of the EGFR kinase domain leads to an acceleration of its phosphorylation, potentiating EGFR kinase activity in an autocatalytic fashion.
source: However, phosphorylation of the conserved regulatory tyrosine Y845 in the activation loop of the EGFR kinase domain leads to an acceleration of its phosphorylation, potentiating EGFR kinase activity in an autocatalytic fashion (Shan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and is consistent with the experimental data showing increased Y845 phosphorylation with EGFR expression.

claim: An autocatalytic activation system coupled to PTP activity offers robustness against biological noise and conveys external stimuli into threshold-activated responses.
source: Such an autocatalytic activation system that is coupled to PTP activity, by for example a double negative feedback, offers robustness against biological noise and conveys external stimuli into threshold-activated responses (Grecco et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and is consistent with the mathematical modeling results.

claim: Autocatalysis can lead to amplified self-activation of the receptor in the absence of a cognate ligand, requiring high PTP activity at the plasma membrane (PM) to suppress.
source: Autocatalysis can lead to amplified self-activation of the receptor in the absence of a cognate ligand (Verveer, 2000; Endres et al., 2013), requiring high PTP activity at the plasma membrane (PM) to suppress.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and the mathematical modeling showing the need for high PTP activity to suppress autocatalysis.

claim: PTP1B and TCPTP act on EGFR with high catalytic efficiency (~2 orders of magnitude higher than EGFR).
source: Such PTPs that act on EGFR with high catalytic efficiency (~2 orders of magnitude higher than EGFR) are PTP1B and TCPTP (Zhang et al., 1993; Romsicki et al., 2003; Fan et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PTP1B and TCPTP are segregated from the PM by association with the cytoplasmic membrane leaflet of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: These PTPs are, however, segregated from the PM by association with the cytoplasmic membrane leaflet of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER)
evidence: This is established knowledge about PTP1B and TCPTP localization.

claim: PTP1B and TCPTP mostly dephosphorylate endocytosed ligand-bound EGFR.
source: and therefore mostly dephosphorylate endocytosed ligand-bound EGFR.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial segregation of these PTPs from the PM and is supported by the experimental data showing EGFR-PTP1B interaction in perinuclear regions.

claim: After ligand binding, endocytosed receptor-ligand complexes contained in clathrin-coated vesicles (CCVs) enter early endosomes (EEs) by fusion.
source: After ligand binding, endocytosed receptor-ligand complexes contained in clathrin-coated vesicles (CCVs) enter early endosomes (EEs) by fusion (Vieira et al., 1996; Bucci et al., 1992; Goh and Sorkin, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Early endosomes further mature in the perinuclear area to late endosomes (LEs) and eventually fuse to lysosomes where receptors are degraded.
source: further maturing in the perinuclear area to late endosomes (LEs) and eventually fusing to lysosomes where receptors are degraded (Rink et al., 2005; Ceresa, 2006; Vanlandingham and Ceresa, 2009; Levkowitz et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Little is known about the role of vesicular trafficking in suppressing spontaneous EGFR activation as well as regulating its signaling response.
source: Although EGFR vesicular trafficking was extensively studied after ligand stimulation, little is known about the role of vesicular trafficking in suppressing spontaneous EGFR activation as well as regulating its signaling response.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Y845 is a regulatory autocatalytic tyrosine whose phosphorylation increases EGFR activity.
source: 1) Y845—a regulatory autocatalytic tyrosine whose phosphorylation increases EGFR activity (Shan et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Y1045 is a site that upon phosphorylation affects vesicular trafficking of EGFR by binding the E3 ligase c-Cbl that ubiquitinates the receptor.
source: 2) Y1045—a site that upon phosphorylation affects vesicular trafficking of EGFR by binding the E3 ligase c-Cbl that ubiquitinates the receptor (Levkowitz et al., 1998)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Y1068 is a site that upon phosphorylation binds the adapter Grb2 via its SH2 domain to propagate signals in the cell.
source: 3) Y1068—a site that upon phosphorylation binds the adapter Grb2 via its SH2 domain to propagate signals in the cell (Okutani et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Unliganded monomeric receptors continuously recycle to the PM to suppress autocatalytic activation.
source: We show that spontaneously and ligand-induced EGFR activation gives rise to distinct molecular states that are recognized and processed differently by the endocytic machinery. While unliganded monomeric receptors continuously recycle to the PM to suppress autocatalytic activation
evidence: This is supported by FRAP/FLAP experiments, TAMRA labeling experiments, and Rab11 colocalization data.

claim: Ligand-bound dimeric receptors are ubiquitinated by the E3-ligase c-Cbl that commits them to unidirectional vesicular trafficking toward lysosomes.
source: ligand-bound dimeric receptors are ubiquitinated by the E3-ligase c-Cbl that commits them to unidirectional vesicular trafficking toward lysosomes.
evidence: This is supported by ubiquitination assays, trafficking experiments with EGF stimulation, and experiments with Y1045F mutants.

claim: The route through perinuclear endosomes enables efficient dephosphorylation of ligand-bound EGFR by high local PTP activity to produce a finite signaling response to growth factors.
source: This route through perinuclear endosomes enables their efficient dephosphorylation by high local PTP activity to produce a finite signaling response to growth factors.
evidence: This is supported by FLIM-FRET data showing EGFR-PTP1B interaction in perinuclear regions and the observation of adaptive phosphorylation response.

source: We demonstrate by a compartmental model that ligand-responsive EGFR signaling can only occur in conjunction with suppression of spontaneous autocatalytic EGFR activation if a ligand-induced switch in EGFR trafficking changes its cyclic interaction with spatially partitioned PTPs to a sustained one.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the mathematical modeling results.
